title: In the Shadow of America’s Nuclear Past, a Startup Flips the Switch on a Truck-Sized Reactor
summary: In Atomic City, Idaho — population 52 — the bar regulars sip drinks called atomic bombs and don’t flinch at the nuclear lab down the road. “I live 10 miles away, and I’m fine,” says Vickie O’Haro, who owns the Atomic City Bar & Store. “I’m not glowing in the dark.” That easy acceptance is rare: a March Gallup poll found most Americans still oppose a nuclear plant in their area. But here, on the 900-square-mile Idaho National Laboratory (INL) — nearly the size of Rhode Island — nuclear energy is just part of the landscape. This summer, that landscape shifted. Deployable Energy, a startup, took its test reactor “critical” — achieving a sustained chain reaction for the first time. It’s a crucial milestone that proves the design can work and, eventually, generate electricity. But unlike the massive, costly plants of the 20th century, this is a micro reactor. “It’s something you can put on the back of a truck,” says Maul, the company’s leader. “It is a fundamentally different proposition.” The reactor could power roughly 1,000 homes, not a million. Nuclear optimists envision a future where these reactors are mass-produced and deployed to remote communities, military bases, or energy-hungry AI data centers — all without carbon emissions. President Trump has accelerated permitting, slashing hundreds of pages of regulations. But that speed alarms critics. Edwin Lyman, nuclear power safety director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, says he has “no confidence” in the Department of Energy’s oversight, citing reduced standards around radiation, security, and environmental contamination. Adding to the concern, ProPublica reported that the federal commission overseeing commercial nuclear development has lost hundreds of staff, especially safety experts, due to Trump administration cuts and resignations. The very companies now testing reactors will soon seek approval from that diminished commission. For locals like O’Haro, though, the new reactors are a source of pride. “I think it’s actually pretty cool to be happening in my backyard,” she says. As America’s energy demand surges, the proving grounds in Idaho may determine whether micro reactors become a widespread solution — or a cautionary tale.
why_it_matters: This story highlights the trade-off between fast-tracking new technology to fight climate change and ensuring rigorous safety checks, which will affect your generation's energy future and the environment. It shows how decisions about nuclear innovation can impact everything from local communities to global carbon emissions.

background_read: The Idaho National Laboratory (INL), a U.S. Department of Energy facility sprawling over 900 square miles, has been at the forefront of nuclear research since 1949, including the first reactor to generate usable electricity in 1951.

Nuclear power, which produces carbon-free electricity, has been controversial in the U.S. since accidents at Three Mile Island (1979) and Chernobyl (1986) raised fears about meltdowns and radiation, and a 2023 Gallup poll found 55% of Americans oppose a nuclear plant built near their home.

Micro reactors, like the one tested by startup Deployable Energy, are designed to be small, transportable on trucks, and capable of powering isolated communities or industrial sites, potentially offering a new way to expand clean energy without massive infrastructure.

The Union of Concerned Scientists, a science advocacy group, has been critical of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) — the independent agency that licenses commercial reactors — arguing that budget cuts and staff losses under recent administrations have weakened safety oversight.

ProPublica, a nonprofit investigative newsroom, reported that the NRC had lost hundreds of experts, especially safety staff, amid Trump administration cuts, raising concerns as companies prepare to seek approval for innovative but untested designs.

perspectives.description: Proponents of micro reactors see them as a versatile, carbon-free energy source that can bring reliable power to off-grid communities, reduce dependence on fossil fuels, and create a new manufacturing sector if the design proves successful.

Opponents worry that the push for rapid deployment, combined with a weakened Nuclear Regulatory Commission, may compromise safety; past nuclear accidents show that oversight lapses can have catastrophic, long-lasting consequences for people and the environment.

Nuclear innovation always balances promise and peril: micro reactors could democratize energy access, but the regulatory rollbacks mirror a broader political trend of prioritizing speed and economic growth over precaution, a pattern seen in other emerging technologies.

The next few years will test whether the NRC, despite staff losses, can rigorously evaluate these new designs; if a safety incident occurs, it could stall the entire micro reactor industry, while a flawless record might pave the way for widespread adoption and help meet future energy demands.
